item.title: World's first 300-MW artificial-cavern compressed air energy storage plant connected to grid in China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16 16:33:00
An aerial view of the world's first 300-megawatt artificial-cavern compressed air energy storage power station, Yuanchu No 1, in Northwest China's Gansu Province. Photo: CCTV News The world's first 300-megawatt artificial-cavern compressed air energy storage (CAES) power station has been connected to the grid in Northwest China's Gansu Province, marking a major step in bringing the technology from experimental testing to large-scale engineering applications, CCTV News reported on Monday, citing China Energy Engineering Corporation (China Energy). The project, known as Yuanchu No 1, provides a new engineering example for diversifying China's compressed air energy storage technologies. The station has four air-storage caverns excavated in rock formations about 110 meters underground. It is equipped with a 300-MW generating unit and has an energy storage capacity of 1,800 megawatt-hours. With a round-trip efficiency of 72 percent, the facility can generate electricity continuously for six hours on a single discharge and has a projected annual power output of 600 million kilowatt-hours. Compressed air energy storage works by converting electricity into energy stored in compressed air, which can later be converted back into electricity when needed. Artificially excavated hard-rock caverns offer an alternative to natural underground storage spaces such as salt caverns. Suitable rock formations are more widely distributed, allowing greater flexibility in site selection, although construction costs are relatively high, according to a report by China Electric Power News published on the website of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Engineering Thermophysics. The report noted that suitable salt formations are concentrated in parts of central, eastern and southern China, while the country's northern regions, which have extensive wind and solar power installations and strong demand for large-scale energy storage, lack suitable geological conditions for salt cavern storage. The Gansu project reached a key testing milestone in September, when an initial air-injection test at its No. 4 underground storage cavern succeeded, with pressure reaching 12.63 mega-pascals, setting a record for compressed air storage in large artificial caverns, according to China Energy. The grid connection comes amid rapid growth in China's new energy storage sector. The country's installed new energy storage capacity reached 136 million kilowatts by the end of 2025, up 84 percent from a year earlier, according to the National Energy Administration (NEA). Lithium-ion batteries accounted for 96.1 percent of the total, while compressed air storage, flow batteries, flywheels and other technologies made up the remaining 3.9 percent. Energy storage projects with a duration of four hours or longer accounted for 27.6 percent of total installed capacity, up about 12 percentage points from the end of 2024, the NEA said. China is also seeking to diversify its energy storage technologies under its development plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). The plan, jointly issued by the National Development and Reform Commission and the NEA, sets a target of 300 million kilowatts of installed new energy storage capacity by 2030, with an average storage duration of about three hours. item.title: China-ASEAN FTA 3.0 to take effect, unlocking new opportunities in AI, green development, supply chain cooperation: MOFCOM
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16 15:52:00
Ministry of Commerce of China File photo: VCG The China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol will enter into force on December 1, 2026. An official from China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) said on Monday that the upgraded deal goes beyond traditional trade and investment liberalization and facilitation of the 1.0 and 2.0 versions to cover emerging areas including digital economy, green development, standards cooperation and supply-chain connectivity, achieving a significant upgrade from "market opening" to "institutional cooperation". Speaking of what the 3.0 version of FTA brings to China and ASEAN and the world, the official said that in an uncertain global economic and trade environment, it will create a more open, convenient, safe, stable and predictable regional market and industrial chain and supply chain system, which will be a practical example of regional cooperation in addressing global challenges. In term of how to conduct future work, the official said that the MOFCOM will support local governments and industries in organizing targeted outreach and training so that enterprises can fully understand the new rules and proactively seize the opportunities created by the upgraded protocol, adding that China will work with ASEAN through the China-ASEAN FTA Joint Committee to set up sub-committees on digital economy, green development, standards and small and medium-sized enterprises. The two sides will review relevant provisions under the protocol's future work plan and hold further consultations on areas such as the digital economy and artificial intelligence (AI). Meanwhile, the upgraded protocol is expected to create multiple new opportunities for enterprises across many fields, including the digital economy, green economy, supply-chain connectivity, as well as customs procedures and trade facilitation, the MOFCOM official said. Regarding the digital economy, the two sides have established the highest-level economic and trade rules and cooperation arrangements in their respective treaty practices. Cooperation will cover both "hard connectivity" in logistics and digital infrastructure and "soft connectivity" in areas such as electronic invoices, electronic payments and electronic bills of lading. The protocol also includes cooperation on AI and other emerging technologies. The official said that these measures will help build an open, secure, stable and predictable digital trade and investment environment, empowering a regional market of nearly 2.1 billion people and its industrial and supply chains. In supply-chain connectivity, the protocol includes a standalone chapter on supply-chain cooperation for the first time in a free trade agreement between the two sides, with high-level commitments. With the continuous deepening of the China-ASEAN FTA, China has remained ASEAN's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has been China's largest trading partner for six consecutive years. By 2025, the trade volume between the two sides will exceed $1 trillion, an increase of 18 times compared to the initial stage of the China-ASEAN FTA in 2002, according to MOFCOM. Global Times

item.title: Chinese medical team offers free consultations, diabetes screening in Tanzania's Zanzibar
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16 11:03:00
A doctor with the 36th Chinese medical team to Tanzania's Zanzibar gives a lecture on diabetes prevention and management to local residents on Pemba Island, Zanzibar, Tanzania, Nov. 14, 2026. (The 36th Chinese medical team to Tanzania's Zanzibar/Handout via Xinhua) The 36th Chinese medical team to Tanzania's Zanzibar on Saturday provided free medical consultations and diabetes screening to residents of Pemba Island as part of activities marking World Diabetes Day. The team's Pemba branch conducted the outreach at Tironi Community Health Point in Mkoani District, South Pemba Region, as part of China's "100 Medical Teams in 1,000 Villages" program. It combined diabetes awareness education with multidisciplinary medical services to improve healthcare access in underserved communities. During the event, Chinese internal medicine physician He Yanhong educated residents on diabetes risk factors, blood glucose monitoring, healthy diets, physical exercise, medication adherence, and the early identification of complications affecting the eyes, kidneys, and feet. The medical team also provided free blood glucose and blood pressure checks, consultations and basic medicines. Specialists in internal medicine, surgery, obstetrics and gynecology, pediatrics, orthopedics, ear, nose and throat, anesthesiology and radiology attended to residents, offering individual treatment plans and health advice. Haji Bakar Haji, an official from Mkoani district health authorities, said the initiative addressed healthcare challenges facing remote communities, where residents often travel long distances to access medical services and receive follow-up care for chronic illnesses. He said the outreach had raised public awareness of diabetes prevention while reducing the financial burden of seeking medical attention. Wang Shu, deputy leader of the 36th Chinese medical team to Zanzibar and head of its Pemba branch, said the team would continue organizing mobile medical consultations, chronic disease awareness campaigns and training for local healthcare workers. He said the activities aimed to strengthen grassroots healthcare services, improve local capacity to prevent and manage chronic diseases, and deepen China-Tanzania cooperation in the health sector. World Diabetes Day is observed annually on Nov. 14 to raise global awareness about diabetes. This chronic disease occurs when the body cannot produce enough insulin or effectively use the insulin it produces, resulting in elevated blood glucose levels.

item.title: Symposium in New York honors Edgar Snow's legacy as bridge builder between China, US
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-16 09:29:00
People attend a symposium themed "The Bridge Builder: Remembering Edgar Snow's Journey 90 Years Ago" in New York, the United States, Nov. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo) Scholars and representatives from China and the United States gathered in New York on Saturday for a symposium honoring Edgar Snow, the American journalist whose pioneering reporting helped introduce the Chinese revolution in the 1930s to the world and whose legacy continues to inspire efforts to foster mutual understanding between the two countries. The symposium, themed "The Bridge Builder: Remembering Edgar Snow's Journey 90 Years Ago," brought together nearly 100 participants, including Snow's family members, representatives of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation (USA), and Chinese and U.S. scholars on Snow studies. In 1936, at the age of 31, Snow broke through blockades and ventured deep into China's impoverished northwest to interview the Red Army. His reporting resulted in the groundbreaking book "Red Star Over China." After the founding of the People's Republic of China, he made three reporting trips to the country, opening a new window on "Red China" to the international community. At Saturday's symposium, speakers shared their reflections on Snow's historical contributions and contemporary influences, highlighting the enduring relevance of his efforts to bridge cultural divides and help the world gain a better understanding of China. People visit a photo exhibition honoring Edgar Snow in New York, the United States, Nov. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo) President of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation Sidne Ward recalled a study tour this summer with Snow's relatives, international representatives and scholars retracing part of Snow's 1936 interview journey in Shaanxi and Ningxia. "It makes me feel more connected to him and to his experiences 90 years ago," she said. For Nancy Hill, president emeritus of the Edgar Snow Memorial Foundation, Snow has many different legacies as a premier journalist and a bridge builder. "He saw the plight of the Chinese people and cared. And he reported that story with his head but also with his heart. I think that's a really beautiful lesson that people can learn from," Hill said. Sun Hua, director of the China Center for Edgar Snow Studies at Peking University, viewed the pursuit of truth, respect for other cultures and a spirit of dedication as Snow's most precious spiritual legacy. "The reason 'Red Star Over China' has remained enduringly significant for 90 years lies in its authenticity and its unvarnished, first-hand source material. That is truly unparalleled. To this day, it remains one of the most authoritative works on the early history of the CPC," Sun said.

item.title: Once again, China's youth are 'stepping up to the plate'!: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 22:30:00
China's youth have become trailblazers Illustration:Xia Qing/GT From the pioneers of the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" program who blazed a trail through the Gobi Desert, to today's youth taking up the torch to tackle challenges in various emerging fields, what has changed is the arena, but what remains unchanged is the innate spirit of never giving up and daring to strive - a spirit ingrained in the blood of the Chinese people. Today's Chinese youth possess greater confidence and capability. Rather than settling for being followers, they have become trailblazers setting trends in emerging new frontier sectors. The 2026 League of Legends World Championship concluded in New York in the early hours of November 15, Beijing Time. Chinese team, Bilibili Gaming (BLG), defeated South Korea's Gen.G to claim the championship title in this esports tournament, which boasts the largest global participation and the highest level of competition. Related topics immediately went viral across major domestic social media platforms, while media from multiple countries rushed to cover the event. Esports is an arena for the young. The average age of BLG's players is early 20s, and the tournament's core audience also consists largely of young people. By fully showcasing their talents on the global stage, they have not only raised the international profile of China's youth but also opened a window into the world of today's young people. BLG's road to the title was, in many ways, a battle to prove its doubters wrong. Before the tournament, much of the global esports community had little faith in the competitiveness of China's League of Legends teams, and BLG itself had an underwhelming group-stage performance. But after advancing to the knockout stage, the team first defeated South Korea's T1, a powerhouse that had maintained an unbeaten record against Chinese teams for 13 years. Then, despite falling behind early in the final, BLG fought back to overcome Gen.G, the top seed from the South Korean league and one of the tournament favorites. In doing so, it helped dispel the long-standing perception that Chinese teams were unable to overcome their South Korean rivals. A documentary released by the club after the victory offered a glimpse into what it took to reach the top. It showed players enduring years of repetitive, demanding training during their academy days, as well as the difficult periods when the team struggled and few believed in its prospects. Clips from the documentary quickly spread across social media. BLG's determination to push through setbacks and prove its critics wrong has struck a chord with young people, many of whom share a desire to challenge prejudice and let their achievements speak for themselves. Looking beyond the esports arena, there is a much broader world where the younger generation is also making its mark. The DeepSeek team consists of fewer than 140 people, with an average age of about 28; more than 75 percent were born in the 1990s, and over half were born after 1995. For the "Beidou" satellite network, the average age of the satellite development team was 31. For the "Chang'e" lunar soil sampling mission, the average age of the heads of key telemetry, tracking, and command positions was 33. For the "Tiangong" space station construction, the average age of the Mengtian lab module final assembly team was 33. And for the "Tianwen" Mars exploration mission, the average age of the flight control team was just 30. A former administrator of the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) once remarked publicly that one of China's space program's greatest strengths lies in the large number of young scientists and engineers it possesses. The Washington Post also noted that "while China's older tech pioneers tend to idolize Silicon Valley," China's younger generation find their role models in people such as DeepSeek's Liang Wenfeng and Unitree's Wang Xingxing. The fact that China's young people are capable of shouldering major responsibilities is winning admiration across the world. For a long time, the ideals of solidarity, hard work and bringing honor to the country were most commonly associated with traditional sports, factory floors, laboratories and fields across the country. But as the digital economy has grown rapidly, a new generation of young Chinese has come of age in new emerging fields, including esports, e-commerce, livestreaming, trendy Chinese cultural products, AI, and green energy. These fields share a common characteristic: rapid knowledge evolution and a high density of innovation. Unlike traditional sectors that require long-term experience and expertise, in these emerging fields, young people often have an edge due to their familiarity with new rules and their sensitivity to technological trends. They do not have to follow the paths paved by their predecessors to the letter; instead, they can compete directly with their global peers on newly opened tracks, and even overtake them by leveraging more flexible thinking and stronger learning abilities. From the pioneers of the "Two Bombs, One Satellite" program (China's successful detonation of an atomic bomb, its first intercontinental ballistic missile, and its first artificial satellite) who blazed a trail through the Gobi Desert, to today's youth taking up the torch to tackle challenges in various emerging fields, what has changed is the arena, but what remains unchanged is the innate spirit of never giving up and daring to strive - a spirit ingrained in the blood of the Chinese people. In the past, when people spoke of "stepping up to the plate," they often referred to hardship, sacrifice, and perseverance. Today's young Chinese not only embody these qualities, but also demonstrate the poise to engage with the world on equal footing, alongside an open-minded and collaborative spirit. Supported by decades of popularized basic education, expanded higher education access, sustained growth in R&D investment, and the accumulated strengths of a complete industrial system, today's Chinese youth possess greater confidence and capability. Rather than settling for being followers, they have become trailblazers setting trends in emerging new frontier sectors. As more and more teams, whose members average in their 20s and 30s, step into the spotlight of the world's top fields, the future of this nation naturally gains its most solid foundation. What the outside world sees in BLG's championship victory is not only the triumph of one esports team, but also the ambition, vigor, and confidence of a nation's younger generation. The vibrant, upward-striving energy of youth is precisely the moving underlying force driving China's continuous progress.

item.title: GT Voice: US chip curb debate cannot stymie China's AI progress
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 22:13:00
Production of semiconductor chip File photo: VCG Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC), China's largest contract chipmaker, reported a 123.4 percent year-on-year increase in net profit attributable to shareholders in the third quarter of 2026. Its performance reflects a broader trend in China's semiconductor industry, where growing market demand is translating into stronger commercial returns. Even if Washington tightens chip export restrictions further, China's artificial intelligence (AI) industry now rests on a firmer industrial foundation than a few years ago. Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia's CEO has sparked intense debate in recent days over its implications for US technology policy. Some observers said that his exit could weaken the chip industry's influence in Washington. Given that many American chip companies have argued that their products should be allowed into China on commercial grounds, Huang's resignation could leave those commercial interests with a less influential voice in Washington, giving greater sway to overblown national security arguments that are increasingly influencing US technology policy. The political tug-of-war over US chip exports to China has been intense in Washington, but its impact on China's AI development may prove increasingly limited. Years of tightening export controls have accelerated China's efforts to build an AI industry that can stand on its own, with far less reliance on American chips. The result is an industry increasingly capable of moving forward without access to American technology. This resilience is built in China thanks to many years' strenuous efforts by Chinese companies. Huawei, Cambricon and other Chinese chipmakers are constantly expanding their presence in the market, while Chinese technology companies are adapting their AI models and computing systems to a growing range of homegrown processors. Together, these developments are giving China an increasingly self-sustaining AI computing ecosystem, making the industry less vulnerable to external restrictions and less dependent on access to US technology. An important part of this picture is China's AI boom, which is opening up new commercial opportunities for its technology industry, including Chinese chipmakers. As demand grows, companies across the semiconductor supply chain have a massive market to expand their businesses and invest in research, development and innovation. SMIC, for instance, spent $258.4 million on research and development in the third quarter alone. This creates a virtuous cycle: the expanding AI market gives domestic chipmakers greater space to grow, generating revenues and profits that can be ploughed back into R&D. Such investment strengthens China's semiconductor industry and, in turn, supports its broader AI development. The progress China's AI industry has made in recent years demonstrates the strength of this cycle, even as the US has tightened its chip restrictions. The harder Washington tightens its technology restrictions, the more complicated the consequences could bring to the US itself. Reuters reported on Friday that Southeast Asia's chip and data center industries expect greater US scrutiny as Washington considers extending export controls. Whether or not these reports translate into policy, the possibility of broader US controls could prompt more Asian economies to reassess their dependence on American technology and accelerate their efforts to diversify their supply chains. This could create new opportunities for Chinese chipmakers, as regional economies seek to broaden their source of chip supplies. And, there could be growing difficulties facing Nvidia and other US chipmakers in the years to come. The growing uncertainty surrounding American chip export controls is increasingly becoming a burden on the industry Washington seeks to "protect." It is also a predicament that post-Huang's Nvidia has to confront. The semiconductor industry is built on deeply intertwined supply chains. Further US export controls could affect chipmakers and technology sectors in Asia, including China, but US companies may be among the first to bear the cost. Whatever the noises Washington makes, China's AI industry will move forward and keep gathering pace. Global Times

item.title: Chinese scientists identify 'fairy circles' in northern China's drylands for the first time and propose how they form
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 21:43:00
Fairy circles photographed by the research team near Alxa Left Banner, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region Photo: Courtesy of Yu Kailiang Chinese scientists have recently identified fairy circles, unusual ring-shaped patterns with sparse vegetation or bare in centers, for the first time in northern China's arid regions and used phase transition theory from statistical physics to explain how the circles may have formed in these drylands, the Global Times learned from the research group on Sunday. The joint research conducted by the research team led by Yu Guirui, an academician of the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), in collaboration with researchers from the Lanzhou University and Gansu Agricultural University, was published in the international academic journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on November 11 local time. Found in the arid regions of Namibia and Australia, fairy circles are unusual ring-shaped patterns in which vegetation flourishes around the edges but is sparse or absent in the center. In China, previous fairy circle research had focused largely on coastal salt marshes, with no confirmed existence in arid and semi-arid regions. The research team studied precipitation gradients along the edges of sandy areas and deserts in northern China, used drones to capture high-resolution images and conducted field surveys. They discovered these patterns, formed by hollow rings of shrubs, at the boundaries between shrublands and grasslands. According to Sun Jingyao, first author of the research paper and postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, the discovery marks the first confirmed record of fairy circles in China's arid regions, alongside with the mechanisms behind their formation being identified as well. Challenging conventional explanations that attribute fairy circles to termite activity or biomass-water feedbacks, the study applies phase transition theory to ecology, suggesting that the patterns emerge naturally when ecosystems reach a critical state, Sun said. Sun explained that phase transition theory, a branch of physics, examines abrupt changes in matter as it shifts from one state or phase to another, and the critical behavior associated with these changes. The researchers used mathematical modeling to demonstrate that fairy circles represent a spatially partitioned "metastable state" in which shrubs and grasses coexist amid intense competition for resources. Sun explained that as precipitation increases and competition from grasses intensifies, the centers of shrub patches become bare due to water scarcity, forming hollow spaces. These hollow rings, in turn, help collect water and sustain the survival of the shrubs. Phase transition theory enables researchers to explain fairy circles and look for early warning signs of ecological collapse along desert margins. Yu Kailiang, corresponding author of the research paper and a research fellow at the institute, told the Global Times on Sunday that fairy circles and vegetation patch expansion were previously treated as isolated natural phenomena and studied separately. However, this study links these phenomena through physical principles, demonstrating that seemingly different abrupt ecological shifts are all manifestations of the same underlying organizational mechanism. It also offers a testable framework for identifying spatial warning signs of potential ecosystem collapse, Yu said.

item.title: The AI summit that got derailed: What Dublin reveals about Europe's waning power
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-15 19:22:00
EU Illustration: Xia Qing/GT On November 13, EU leaders gathered in Dublin for a summit the outside world had been watching closely, devoted substantially to artificial intelligence (AI). But as the summit unfolded, the Ukraine issue was abruptly thrust onto the agenda - in the wake of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner's meeting with Zelensky the day prior to the summit - becoming the summit's main focus. European leaders had to put AI aside and discuss how to form a negotiating team and "speak with one voice" to the outside world. On the surface, the US stole the show. But looking through this disrupted agenda, we see a more authentic Europe. This is not just about an agenda being hijacked; it shows how today's Europe repeatedly wavers between "security" and "prosperity." Why did security override prosperity? Because the pain of these two issues is fundamentally different. The pain of Ukraine is immediate; it hurts today and will hurt tomorrow. Funding gaps remain, a 22nd round of sanctions is coming, and the November 26 Council meeting will require more financial discussions. The fear that the US and Russia might negotiate behind closed doors and arrange Europe's fate is a terror that cashes out instantly. By contrast, the pain of AI lies 10 to 20 years in the future. No one can accurately calculate the votes a decade from now. Discussing the future requires money, the approval of 27 member states, building gigafactories, and waiting for talent to be deployed. In a system dominated by electoral politics, distant water cannot quench immediate thirst. Yet, it is this "postponed half" that exposes the hollowing out of Europe's power. At the meeting, Ursula von der Leyen said Europe was planning €30 billion (33.07 billion US dollars) to build seven AI "Gigafactories." It sounds like a lot. But to truly gain a foothold in AI, Europe needs at least €500 billion (551.10 billion dollars). Where will this money come from? The meeting didn't say. Because the moment money is mentioned, none of the 27 countries want to pay more. The factories are still on paper. The 2023 Chips Act set a goal to capture 20% of the global market, but the industry has already declared it unattainable. Look further back: The 2000 Lisbon Strategy aimed to build the world's most competitive knowledge economy by 2010. It failed, so it was rebranded as the "Europe 2020 Strategy." When 2020 arrived, it failed again. Why? Because subsidizing farmers and saving factories wins votes; spending money on long-term competitiveness does not. Therefore, whenever it comes to fork out real money, Europe habitually retreats to "coordination." This "informal meeting" didn't even pass a concluding document. It spun its wheels all day, stuck in a loop. Europe remains wealthy and dignified, and its standard of living is high. But in the hard dimensions that dictate the world's future direction - computing power, chips, and AI models - it is retreating. It is plagued by strategic anxiety, leaving it unable to achieve seemingly clear objectives, including shaping the future security landscape. You only become this anxious when you feel you might become a pawn on the chessboard. Leverage at the negotiating table never relies on declarations; it relies on hard power. In the future global landscape, computing power and chips are the hardest currency. Falling behind in this domain means losing a seat in future great power competition. A Europe that cannot stand firmly on its own feet will be entangled in immediate crises, unable to see the long-term direction, and will become more conservative, inward-looking, and more right-wing and extreme. This is hardly good news for a multipolar world. Whether Europe can maintain its strategic autonomy, strive to become a significant force in a multipolar world, and play an independent role in the international order without depending on any third party depends on how much effort it is willing to devote to these goals. What Europe lacks most is not another declaration of "strategic autonomy," but the admission that it is no longer the old, high-and-mighty Europe. It needs reform, openness, and renewed vitality. However, the agenda in Dublin - so easily derailed by Ukraine - demonstrates that taking this crucial first step remains incredibly difficult.
